content_voiceover: This is a big-picture map of how we treat AML in twenty twenty-six, and the whole thing hinges on two questions, is the patient fit for intensive chemotherapy, and does the leukemia have a targetable mutation. Start with the fit patients on the top left. If they have a FLT3 mutation, you add midostaurin or quizartinib to seven plus three. Core binding factor AML often gets gemtuzumab ozogamicin added. Therapy-related or secondary AML does better with CPX-351, the liposomal daunorubicin-cytarabine combination, instead of standard seven plus three. After induction, consolidation is transplant, high-dose cytarabine, or oral azacitidine for maintenance. Now shift to unfit patients, bottom left, the backbone is venetoclax combined with a hypomethylating agent or low-dose cytarabine. If they carry an IDH1 mutation, ivosidenib gets added to that azacitidine backbone. On the right side is the salvage setting for relapsed or refractory disease. Fit patients typically get FLAG-Ida plus or minus venetoclax, while unfit patients get mutation-directed single agents, gilteritinib for FLT3, ivosidenib or enasidenib for IDH1 or IDH2, and revumenib for NPM1 or KMT2A rearranged disease. The gray boxes just flag agents not currently available in Taiwan.
keypoints: Fitness for intensive chemo and mutation status drive first-line choice
FLT3 mutated fit patients get midostaurin or quizartinib added to seven plus three
Unfit patients get venetoclax plus a hypomethylating agent or low-dose cytarabine
IDH1 mutated unfit patients can add ivosidenib to the backbone
Salvage therapy is increasingly mutation-directed, gilteritinib, ivosidenib, enasidenib, revumenib
keypoint_voiceover: Keep two axes in mind, fitness for intensive chemo, and presence of an actionable mutation like FLT3, IDH1, IDH2, or NPM1-KMT2A. Those two axes determine essentially every box on this chart, both in the first-line and salvage settings.
